name: Maya Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Maya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Nothing you say will be linked to your name, so you can be as honest as you like.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I'm not great at talking about myself, but I'll try.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I take two buses to the city university, about fifty minutes each way, and I do my reading on the bus. Mornings are lectures and a programming lab, and I'm usually the one who stays behind to finish the exercise on my own. Saturdays and Sundays I'm at Pemberton's bakery on Harrow Road, serving from six to noon. My mum Dana works nights as a care assistant, so I make dinner for my brother Theo, who's fourteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to be honest. Half my course spent the summer panicking that coding was finished, and I think it was mostly noise. At the bakery I'd tell my boss Gwen that the ovens still need people at five in the morning, same as ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm relieved, but it doesn't fix my real problem. I'm borrowing for fees every term and I have under a month of rent and food saved. My mum still works nights to keep the lights on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my fourteen hours at the bakery and keep writing every assignment by hand. I don't use chatbots, I want to actually learn it. In second year I'd go for a summer placement, because those decide who gets a graduate job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady, mostly. There's a knot underneath about money that never goes away, AI or no AI. I'd probably sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep writing everything by hand. Does that ever cost you anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sometimes. A lab partner finished in half the time last week using a chatbot, and I stayed until nine. But I can explain every line I hand in, and I think that matters when interviews come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of the money worry is biggest right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bus pass and the laptop. Mine is six years old and the fan screams whenever I compile. If it dies, I have no savings to replace it, so I'd have to borrow from my mum's rent money.

say: I'd tell friends the panic was **hype**, and I'm glad I never leaned on chatbots.
At the bakery I'd say the ovens still need **people** at five in the morning.
think: I'm relieved, but my **loan** keeps growing whatever AI does.
Under a month of savings means one broken **laptop** is a crisis.
do: Keep working **fourteen hours** a week at Pemberton's bakery.
Write every coding assignment myself, with no chatbot shortcuts.
Apply for a **summer placement** at the end of first year.
feel: Mostly **steady**, with a money knot underneath that never goes away.
S0.quote: I'm borrowing for fees every term and I have under a month of rent and food saved.
fieldNote: Relief is real but quickly replaced by **money** talk; her stress comes from debt and a six-year-old laptop, not AI.
Refuses **AI tools** on principle and accepts the slower pace as the price.
Clearly the **carer** for her brother Theo, which limits her time.

steps.text: Keep working Saturday and Sunday shifts at Pemberton's bakery
Put aside a little from each wage for a laptop fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the companies are using it as an excuse to hire fewer juniors, and that somebody should make them train people. I'd back the student union if it pushed for that. At the bakery I'd probably just say prices on the till system are about to go up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this one scares me. Coding and checking are exactly the tasks it takes first, and those are the entry jobs I'm studying for. I think the firms will hire fewer graduates and expect the rest to do twice the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the course and push for the best marks I can, since a top result is my edge. I'd join the student union's campaign on graduate hiring and ask my tutor which modules are about checking AI, not competing with it. I'd keep the bakery job through the holidays so I don't have to borrow more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a bit angry too. I don't trust that there's time to adjust for people like me, because adjusting costs money and I have none behind me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't use AI tools. How do you square that with a world where everyone does?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know, it's a contradiction. I think I'll have to learn at some point, but I want the basics solid first, so that I'm not just pressing a button. If I'm pushed, I'd do it through a university course, not on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you blame if graduate jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech firms and the managers who sign off on cutting junior roles to save money. Not the AI itself. A union for software workers would be a start.

say: I'd say firms are using AI as an excuse to hire fewer **juniors**.
I'd back the student union if it campaigned on **graduate hiring**.
think: Coding and checking are exactly the **entry jobs** I'm studying for, and that scares me.
Adjusting costs money, and I have **none** behind me.
do: Aim for the **top marks** in every module, since results are my edge.
Join the student union campaign on graduate hiring.
Keep the bakery shifts through holidays to avoid borrowing more.
feel: **Anxious** and angry, because the time to adjust belongs to people with money.
S1.quote: I don't trust that there's time to adjust for people like me, because adjusting costs money and I have none behind me.
fieldNote: Blames **employers** and big tech, not the technology; reaches for collective action first.
Admits her refusal to use AI is a **contradiction** but wants the basics first.
Anxiety is concrete: **entry-level** coding jobs are the ones she expects to shrink.

steps.text: Join the student union campaign on graduate hiring
Keep the weekend bakery shifts through the holidays
Ask my tutor for modules on checking and testing AI output

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's reckless. Two years is nothing, and nobody's voted for this. I'd be posting that the government has to protect people before the companies roll it out, and I'd go to any protest I could get to on a Saturday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my degree might be worth very little by the time I'd finish it. I'd have borrowed for three years and then there'd be no junior jobs. And I haven't even touched these tools, so I feel behind on top of everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably still go to lectures, because what else is there. I'd talk to my mum about whether I should stop borrowing for the second year. I'd also take more bakery hours, because robots for baking come later, around 2031, and I'd want some money in the bank while it still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be lying awake. The honest feeling is that I picked the wrong thing and have nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, what would your mum say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum would say finish what you started and she'd work extra nights, which is exactly what I don't want. I'd rather get a trade qualification quickly than make my mum work even more nights for a degree that might be worth nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to use the AI tools in that case?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably yes, because refusing would be pointless. I'd hate it, but I'd sit down with the university's free course and treat it as survival, not as something I like.

say: I'd call it **reckless**, since nobody voted for it and two years is nothing.
I'd go to any **protest** I could reach on a Saturday.
think: My degree may be worth **very little** by the time I finish.
I haven't touched these tools, so I feel **behind** on top of it.
do: Talk to my mum about whether to stop **borrowing** for second year.
Take extra bakery hours to build savings while the work still pays.
Enrol on the university's free course on using AI tools.
feel: **Alarmed**, lying awake with a sense of having picked the wrong thing.
S2.quote: I'd rather get a trade qualification quickly than make my mum work even more nights for a degree that might be worth nothing.
fieldNote: Shift from union anger to personal **alarm**; the two-year window makes her debt feel pointless.
Considers dropping the degree for a **trade**, mainly to protect her mother.
Reluctantly reverses her **no-AI** stance, framing it as survival.

steps.text: Go to protests on Saturdays when the bakery rota allows
Take extra bakery hours and bank the wages
Sit the university's free course on using AI tools
Look into a short electrician course instead of year two

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something sensible, but only if governments act now. I'd tell people on my course to join the union side of this, and not only worry. I'd probably be quiet at the bakery, since nobody there thinks about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd just about make it through the degree before things change. The worry is the first job. I'd be a new graduate in 2030, when the thinking work is nearly all done by machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree but choose modules that lead to hands-on engineering, like embedded systems and hardware, because robots for hands-on work come later, around 2034. I'd also start using an AI tool for small things, with my tutor's approval, so I'm not the only one who can't. And I'd save from every wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have something to hold on to. Five years feels like a decision I can make, not a thing that hits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned hardware. Why would that feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A machine can write code, but somebody still has to wire things and fix them on site. My uncle Karim is an electrician and he says the work doesn't stop. It's a bet, but it's the one I'd make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your brother Theo in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd be nineteen when it lands. I'd try to talk him into something practical and not let him drift into a screen job. I'd also want Mum to start a small pension again, she stopped when we had no money.

say: I'd say five years is enough to act, **if** governments start now.
I'd tell coursemates to push through the **union**, not just worry.
think: I'd scrape through the degree, but the **first job** in 2030 is the danger.
Five years feels like a **decision** I can make, not something that just hits.
do: Choose modules in **embedded systems** and hardware, where robots arrive later.
Try one AI tool for small tasks, with my tutor's approval.
Save part of every bakery wage.
feel: **Anxious**, but with something to hold on to.
S3.quote: A machine can write code, but somebody still has to wire things and fix them on site.
fieldNote: The longer window turns her anxiety into a **plan**: hardware modules over pure software.
Brings in **family**: her uncle's trade is her model for safe work.
Still **cautious** with AI, now willing to test it with a tutor's backing.

steps.text: Pick embedded systems and electronics modules for second year
Try one AI tool on small lab tasks with my tutor's okay
Save a fixed share of each bakery wage every week
Steer my brother Theo towards a practical trade or engineering route

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it, and a waste if they don't. I'd write to my local councillor about retraining money and I'd support the union side. At the bakery I'd tell Gwen she should get the ordering done on a simple app before somebody makes her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the degree is probably fine and my first jobs will be different from what the course says. Maybe I'll end up doing the human parts: checking, safety, explaining things to customers. I could even do a masters later if there's funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree properly, take the placement, and start learning AI tools in second year, slowly. I'd pay down the loan only as far as the rules require, since there'd be time. I'd also join the student union committee, because ten years is long enough for a campaign to actually change things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's still big, but there's room to breathe. I'd stop feeling like the whole thing might fall on me before I'm ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having ten years change how you feel about using AI yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. With ten years I can learn it carefully and decide what I'm not comfortable with. With two I'd just grab whatever works. I prefer being slow, and this lets me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to be doing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe running a small team that tests software for hospitals, where mistakes matter. It's the kind of work I'd want a person to be responsible for, and I'd like to be that person.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if people use it and a waste if they don't.
I'd write to my local councillor about **retraining money**.
think: The degree is probably **fine**, but the first jobs will look different from the course.
I might end up doing the human parts: **checking**, safety and explaining.
do: Take the **placement** and learn AI tools slowly from second year.
Join the student union committee and push for graduate support.
Keep the bakery job and avoid extra borrowing.
feel: **Uneasy**, but with room to breathe and time to prepare.
S4.quote: Ten years is a gift if people use it, and a waste if they don't.
fieldNote: Her slow, careful style finally fits the **timeline**; ten years suits her.
Imagines a **human-responsibility** role such as testing software for hospitals.
Still **political**: wants councillors and union action, not only personal plans.

steps.text: Write to my local councillor about funded retraining for adults
Learn one AI tool slowly during second year
Join the student union committee and push on graduate jobs
Keep the weekend bakery shifts to avoid extra loans

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, no question. Two years isn't enough for my mum, my brother or me to do anything properly, and I'd be borrowing for a degree that might not count. What would help is a real government plan before it happens, a union for tech workers, and fees that stop if the jobs don't appear.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people assume students like me are all fine because we got good grades. I got the grades, and I still count the coins for my bus pass. Please say that part.

headlineQuote: I got the grades, and I still count the coins for my bus pass.
portrait: **Maya** is an eighteen-year-old computing student who works weekends at a bakery and cooks for her brother.
She refuses **AI tools** on principle and blames employers and big tech rather than the technology.
Money shapes every answer: a thin cushion and growing **loan** make even the calm scenario uneasy.
With two years she turns **alarmed** and considers a trade; with five or ten she plans around hardware and unions.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because two years is too short for her family to adjust and her loan would be pointless.
whatWouldHelp: A real **government plan** before it happens, a union for tech workers, and fees that stop if graduate jobs vanish.
